One more task on this level. We compared your analysis with the actual game engine. The engine has a cheaper
winning route than your analysis allows: at least one rule you assumed forbids, or charges more for, a move that
the engine allows. I am not telling you which rule, or anything about the true cost. Find the discrepancy yourself.
This tells you only that your least cost is too high. It does not tell you whether the level can be won within its
budget: the true least cost may still be above the budget, or it may not.

Your bound holds only under the rules as you understood them. If one of those rules is looser than the game, your
least cost can only be too low. If one of them is stricter than the game - it
forbids a move the game allows, or charges more for it - your least cost is too high and your conclusion about
whether the level can be won may be wrong, and your own reasoning cannot show this. So work out which of your rules your least cost depends on,
and test those rules in the game, especially in situations you have never played. Situations that your analysis
told you were not worth playing are the most likely place for such an error.

   **Refill collection during enlargement:** I had allowed collection only through small-piece movement. In attempt 1, enlarging small (25,33) into large (23,31) collected the refill: net spending changed from 10 to 5 after the five-unit spell and ten-unit refill. Attempt 2 separated this from ordinary visual overlap: moving large (25,33)→(21,33) cost one unit, 5→6, without collecting it. Enlarging small (27,33)→large (25,31) also failed to collect it, costing 13→18. Attempt 4 confirmed another successful enlargement pickup, (25,35)→(23,33), with spending 11→6. Thus enlargement can collect the refill, but proximity or visible overlap alone does not explain when.

   **Enlargement placement:** I had required displacement (−2,−2), rejecting enlargement if that placement was blocked. In attempt 3, small (21,35) successfully became large (21,33), costing 9→14. This boundary test distinguished rejection from finding another placement. The displacement was (0,−2).
